OptiSparseMET: Robust Design of Sparse Multi-Environment Trials

Source: vignettes/OptiSparseMET-introduction.Rmd
OptiSparseMET-introduction.Rmd

1. Introduction

1.1 The core problem

A multi-environment trial (MET) evaluates candidate genotypes across the target population of environments (TPE), defined by locations, years, or location-by-year combinations, to support selection for broad or specific adaptation. In modern breeding programmes, however, the number of candidates JJ usually exceeds the plot capacity of any one environment. Complete testing of all JJ genotypes in all II environments is therefore infeasible.

Sparse testing addresses this constraint by observing only a planned subset of genotype-by-environment cells. The scientific problem is not simply to omit cells, but to determine which omissions preserve information about genetic merit and genotype-by-environment interaction (G×E). The operational problem is simultaneously to respect local field geometry, heterogeneous site capacity, and a finite network-wide seed inventory.

Accordingly, an effective sparse MET must achieve three objectives: (i) retain direct and model-assisted genetic connectivity; (ii) allocate replication where it contributes most to prediction and selection; and (iii) produce field books that can be planted without exceeding plots or seed.

1.2 What OptiSparseMET does

OptiSparseMET addresses sparse MET design at two linked levels:

  1. Across-environment allocation — which lines go to which environments, how many times each line is replicated across the trial, and whether the resulting connectivity is sufficient for cross-environment inference.

  2. Within-environment design — how the lines assigned to each environment are arranged in the field, how checks are distributed, how blocks control local heterogeneity, and how spatial gradients are managed.

The package embeds these levels within an environmental evidence framework. Weather, soil, management, and geographic similarities are retained as separate main-effect kernels, while weather-by-soil, weather-by-management, and soil-by-management kernels represent explicit cross-modality hypotheses. Historical MET responses, when available, calibrate genetic environment covariance. Without such responses, no environmental weights are requested: the identity matrix defines the central covariance, and the separate kernels define unweighted maximin sensitivity scenarios.

The two design levels are therefore linked through (i) the statistical model, (ii) the information matrix that governs prediction precision, and (iii) the physical constraints that determine which local layouts can be implemented.

How the two levels are linked

Link 1 — The incidence matrix couples allocation to estimation. For genotype-by-environment effects uu with prior covariance σg2(ΣE⊗G)\sigma_g^2(\Sigma_E\otimes G), met_information() uses the absorbed random-effect coefficient matrix

Cuu=D−DX(X⊤DX)−1X⊤D+{σg2(ΣE⊗G)}−1.C_{uu}=D-DX(X^\top D X)^{-1}X^\top D+ \{\sigma_g^2(\Sigma_E\otimes G)\}^{-1}.

Here XX represents fixed environment means and DD contains the information from the observed genotype-by-environment cells. Allocation determines which diagonal entries of DD are non-zero; actual replication, residual variance, and within-environment efficiency determine their magnitude. The prior precision couples environments through ΣE\Sigma_E and lines through GG. Prediction error comes from Cuu−1C_{uu}^{-1}, so both design levels affect the selection criterion.

Link 2 — Allocation fixes which within-environment designs are feasible. With allocation incidence MM, the number of distinct lines assigned to environment ee is ke=∑jMjek_e = \sum_j M_{je}. Once allocation is complete, kek_e is fixed. The within-environment design must then arrange exactly kek_e treatments across the available nrows×ncolsn_{\text{rows}} \times n_{\text{cols}} plots. If kek_e is incompatible with the blocking structure — for example, if kek_e is not a multiple of the block size, or if kek_e exceeds field capacity — the within-environment design is infeasible regardless of how good the allocation was. Allocation and field geometry must be co-designed.

Link 3 — Block structure affects cross-environment inference. Consider two environments sharing nsharedn_{\text{shared}} lines. The precision of the cross-environment genetic correlation estimate depends on how well those shared lines are estimated within each environment, which in turn depends on the block efficiency within each environment. Formally, the effective replication of a shared line jj across environments is modulated by the efficiency factor ϵe\epsilon_e of the design in environment ee. In the package’s MET information model, its observation-information contribution is:

dje=rjeϵeσe2d_{je} = \frac{r_{je}\epsilon_e}{\sigma_e^2}

where rjer_{je} is the number of plots for line jj in environment ee and ϵe∈(0,1]\epsilon_e \in (0, 1] is the efficiency factor relative to the chosen reference design. A poor within-environment design (low ϵe\epsilon_e) reduces information and increases prediction error, which degrades G×E inference even when the allocation incidence structure is ideal. The block design within each environment affects the quality of cross-environment comparisons.

Link 4 — The mean coefficient of determination (CDmean) depends on both levels simultaneously. For the chosen genetic target hjh_j (for example, the across-TPE mean), the line-specific coefficient of determination is

CDj=1−PEV(hj)Var(hj),CDmean=1J∑j=1JCDj.CD_j = 1-\frac{\text{PEV}(h_j)}{\text{Var}(h_j)}, \qquad \text{CDmean}=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}CD_j.

The prior variance in the denominator respects both the relationship diagonal and the selected environment target. Prediction-error variance (PEV) depends on allocation and actual cell replication through the absorbed mixed-model information matrix, and on within-environment efficiency. Neither design level can substitute for the other.

Standard MET tools address one level at a time: either choosing an allocation strategy without regard to field feasibility, or constructing within-environment designs without regard to how many lines the allocation will deliver. This leads to inconsistencies — for example, an allocation that requires a non-integer number of blocks per replicate, or a field design that assumes more lines than the allocation provides. OptiSparseMET makes both levels explicit and coordinates them: the allocation output specifies exactly which lines enter each environment, and the within-environment engine receives precisely that set, ensuring that both the incidence structure and the blocking structure are optimised consistently within the same statistical framework.

2. Statistical Framework

2.1 The linear mixed model

Phenotypic observations in plant breeding trials are analysed using a linear mixed model. For a single environment, a typical form is:

y=Xβ+Zg+ey = X\beta + Zg + e

where:

  • yy is the vector of observed phenotypic values (one per plot)
  • XβX\beta captures fixed effects: the overall mean, environment effects, check effects, and any fixed treatment contrasts
  • ZgZg captures random line effects: g∼N(0,Kσg2)g \sim N(0,\, K\sigma_g^2), where KK is a genomic relationship matrix (GRM) or pedigree numerator relationship matrix (A), and σg2\sigma_g^2 is the genetic variance
  • e∼N(0,Rσe2)e \sim N(0,\, R\sigma_e^2) is the vector of residuals, with RR encoding the spatial covariance structure

The design matrix ZZ — whose columns correspond to lines and whose rows correspond to plots — is determined entirely by the experimental design. A good design is one that makes ZZ well-conditioned for estimation.

2.2 Why design affects inference

When ZZ is sparse, not all lines are observed in all environments. Cross-environment inference then depends on either:

  • Design-based connectivity: lines that co-occur in the same environment create direct comparisons; common treatments that appear in every environment create bridges between sites.
  • Model-based connectivity: the relationship matrix KK propagates information between genetically related lines, even if they never appear in the same environment.

Both mechanisms are important, but model-based connectivity is less robust because it depends on the assumed covariance structure being correct. A well-designed sparse MET builds in design-based connectivity as a safeguard.

2.3 Efficiency criteria

Given a design, its statistical efficiency can be measured by how well it supports estimation and prediction of genetic values. The three main criteria used by OptiSparseMET are:

A-optimality minimises the average variance of treatment comparison estimates (contrasts). Formally it minimises trace(C−1)\text{trace}(C^{-1}) where CC is the coefficient matrix of the treatment effects. A lower value is better. Its reciprocal, A-efficiency =1/Acriterion= 1 / A_{\text{criterion}}, is sometimes more interpretable because larger values are better.

D-optimality maximises the determinant of the estimable information matrix, which minimises generalised variance and the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for treatment contrasts. It is more sensitive to the overall spread of information across all contrasts than A-optimality, which focuses on the average. Again, D-efficiency =1/Dcriterion= 1 / D_{\text{criterion}} is used so larger values are better.

CDmean is the criterion most directly tied to genomic prediction. For target genetic value hjh_j, it is defined as:

CDmean=1J∑j=1J{1−PEV(hj)Var(hj)}.\text{CDmean}=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J} \left\{1-\frac{\text{PEV}(h_j)}{\text{Var}(h_j)}\right\}.

The line-specific prior variance can differ through the relationship diagonal and the environment target. The package bounds numerical reliability estimates to [0,1][0,1]; values close to 1 indicate precise prediction. CDmean incorporates both the relationship model and design information.

For novice readers: Think of CDmean as “what fraction of the true genetic value the design allows you to recover on average.” A CDmean of 0.85 means the design, on average, captures 85% of the genetic signal.

3. Two-Level Design Structure

3.1 Across-environment allocation

The resource identity underlying balanced sparse allocation is:

N=J×r=∑e=1IkeN = J \times r = \sum_{e=1}^{I} k_e

where:

Symbol Meaning
NN Total number of line-by-environment observations
JJ Total number of candidate lines
rr Number of environments each line enters (replication depth)
II Number of environments
kek_e Number of lines tested in environment ee (coverage breadth)

Given a fixed total resource NN, this identity formalizes a fundamental tradeoff: increasing coverage breadth (testing more lines per environment, larger kek_e) necessarily reduces replication depth (each line appears in fewer environments, smaller rr). Equal site sizes are the special case ∑eke=Ik\sum_e k_e = I k. No design can simultaneously maximise both.

For novice readers: With 100 lines and 4 environments, 400 line-by-environment slots allow all 100 lines in all 4 environments (r=4r=4, k=100k=100). With 200 slots, testing 50 lines per environment allows each line to appear in 2 environments (r=2r=2, k=50k=50). With 100 slots, testing 25 lines per environment allows each line to appear once (r=1r=1, k=25k=25). In each equal-site example, Jr=IkJr=Ik.

The practical constraint is that kk is bounded by the number of plots available per environment, and rr is bounded by seed availability. The allocation problem is to choose which lines go to which environments, subject to these bounds.

When common treatments are included, a number CC of lines are assigned to every environment before sparse allocation begins. Their count is subtracted from each environment’s capacity:

ke*=ke−Ck_e^* = k_e - C

The sparse-allocatable lines number J*=J−CJ^* = J - C, and the modified resource identity applies to them:

J*×r=∑e=1Ike*J^* \times r = \sum_{e=1}^{I} k_e^*

For equal environment sizes this reduces to J*r=Ik*J^*r=Ik^*.

3.2 Within-environment design

Each environment receives an independent field design constructed by one of two engines:

  • met_prep_famoptg() for block-based repeated-check designs, including augmented, partially replicated (p-rep), and randomised complete block design (RCBD)-type layouts
  • met_alpha_rc_stream() for row-column alpha designs suited to large-scale spatial field structure

The choice between them depends on field geometry, check structure, replication goals, and the spatial model anticipated at analysis. They can differ across environments within the same trial.

4. Pipeline Overview

The OptiSparseMET workflow proceeds in four stages, with an optional shortcut that runs all four together.

STAGE 0   Verify per-environment capacity
          suggest_safe_k()  OR  min_k_for_full_coverage()
          |
STAGE 1   Allocate lines across environments
          allocate_sparse_met()
          |
STAGE 2   Reconcile allocation and replication against one shared inventory
          plan_sparse_met_design()
          (assign_replication_by_seed() remains the local-site helper)
          |
STAGE 3   Build within-environment field designs
          met_prep_famoptg()  OR  met_alpha_rc_stream()
          (optional: evaluate and optimise each design)
          |
STAGE 4   Assemble the combined MET field book
          combine_met_fieldbooks()

          --- OR: run stages 1-4 together ---

          plan_sparse_met_design()
library(DiagrammeR)

grViz("
digraph OptiSparseMET {
  graph [layout = dot, rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = rectangle, style = rounded, fontname = Helvetica]

  A [label = 'Input\nLines  Environments\nFamilies / GRM / A\nSeed inventory']
  B [label = 'Stage 0: Verify capacity\nsuggest_safe_k()']
  C [label = 'Stage 1: Allocation\nallocate_sparse_met()\n(M3 or M4)']
  D [label = 'Stage 2: Network seed ledger\nplan_sparse_met_design()']
  E [label = 'Stage 3: Field design\nmet_prep_famoptg()\nor met_alpha_rc_stream()']
  F [label = 'Stage 4: Assemble\ncombine_met_fieldbooks()']
  G [label = 'Outputs\ncombined_field_book\nenvironment_summary\nefficiency_summary']

  A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F -> G
}
")

5. Feasibility Helpers

Before any allocation, it is essential to verify that the chosen per-environment capacity kk is large enough to assign every non-common line at least once. Passing a capacity that is too small causes allocate_sparse_met() to stop with an informative error.

The minimum capacity for full coverage under equal environment sizes is:

kmin=⌈J*I⌉+Ck_{\min} = \left\lceil \frac{J^*}{I} \right\rceil + C

where ⌈⋅⌉\lceil \cdot \rceil is the ceiling function. This is the floor below which any sparse allocation must leave some lines unassigned.

OptiSparseMET provides three helpers:

Function Action
min_k_for_full_coverage() Returns kmink_{\min} exactly
suggest_safe_k() Returns kmink_{\min} plus a user-defined buffer
warn_if_k_too_small() Emits a non-fatal warning if k<kmink < k_{\min}

Always call one of these before allocate_sparse_met().

library(OptiSparseMET)

data("OptiSparseMET_example_data")
x <- OptiSparseMET_example_data

# Strict arithmetic minimum
min_k_for_full_coverage(
  n_treatments_total  = length(x$treatments),    # 120
  n_environments      = length(x$environments),  # 4
  n_common_treatments = length(x$common_treatments)  # 8; J*=112
)
# min_sparse_slots_per_environment = 28  (= ceil(112/4))
# min_total_entries_per_environment = 36 (= 28 + 8)

# Safe value with buffer of 3
suggest_safe_k(
  treatments        = x$treatments,
  environments      = x$environments,
  common_treatments = x$common_treatments,
  buffer            = 3
)
# Returns 39

# Non-fatal check (useful inside scripts)
warn_if_k_too_small(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 39,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments
)
# No warning: 4 * (39 - 8) = 124 >= 112 sparse lines

5.1 Input contract: required and optional data

This section defines the inputs expected by the end-to-end package workflow. A required input has no usable default. A conditional input becomes required only when its associated analysis is requested. Optional evidence can improve a design, but its absence must not be hidden by invented values.

5.1.1 General formatting rules

  1. Treatment and environment identifiers must be non-missing, non-empty, and unique within their defining table.
  2. The same identifier must be written identically in every object. Matching is case-sensitive.
  3. Check treatments are supplied to the local field-design specifications; they are not included in the treatments vector used for sparse allocation.
  4. Named vectors are recommended whenever values differ among environments or treatments. Names, rather than position, then control alignment.
  5. Relationship and covariance matrices must be numeric, finite, square, symmetric, and identically named by row and column.
  6. Seed availability and seed requirement must use the same unit; grams are a common choice. An absent treatment-by-environment cell consumes 0 g.
  7. Missing environmental observations must remain NA until an explicit quality-control and imputation rule is applied.

5.1.2 End-to-end design: plan_sparse_met_design()

Required arguments
Argument Accepted format Requirement
treatments Unique character vector Test-entry IDs. Do not include local checks.
environments Unique character vector of length at least 2 Environment IDs used consistently throughout the design.
n_test_entries_per_environment Positive integer scalar, positional integer vector, or named integer vector Number of distinct test entries at each environment, including common entries but excluding local check plots and extra replication plots.
env_design_specs Named list with one list per environment Local design engine, field dimensions, checks, and engine-specific settings. Names must cover every value in environments.

Example core vectors:

treatments <- sprintf("G%03d", seq_len(120))
environments <- c("Environment_A", "Environment_B", "Environment_C")
n_test_entries_per_environment <- c(
  Environment_A = 80L,
  Environment_B = 60L,
  Environment_C = 60L
)
Optional and conditional arguments
Argument Default When it is used
allocation_method "random_balanced" Use "equireplicate" when equal environment replication and the required degree sequence are feasible. "M3" and "M4" remain aliases.
target_replications Inferred Target number of environments per non-common treatment; strict for equireplicate.
common_treatments NULL Character vector of preselected entries. When supplied, these identities are fixed and required at every environment; their local replication may differ.
balance "none" "env_pair", "line_pair", or "both" for concurrence refinement.
balance_iter, balance_seed 2000L, NULL Iteration budget and reproducibility seed for concurrence refinement.
treatment_info NULL Required for family-guided allocation; also supplies family labels to local designs.
seed_info NULL Activates network-wide seed accounting and seed-aware local replication.
seed_required_per_plot NULL Required with seed_info; scalar, named vector/list, or an environment-level data frame.
minimum_seed_buffer 0 Non-negative reserve retained per treatment after the complete network is planned.
allocation_group_source "none" "Family", "GRM", or "A" activates genetic grouping.
GRM NULL Required when allocation_group_source = "GRM".
A NULL Required when allocation_group_source = "A".
id_map NULL Required only when treatment IDs differ from relationship-matrix IDs.
group_method "kmeans" "kmeans" or "hclust" for matrix-derived allocation groups.
group_seed, group_attempts, n_pcs_use 1, 25, Inf Reproducibility, restarts, and retained principal components for matrix-derived groups.
min_groups_per_environment NULL Minimum represented genetic groups per environment, where feasible.
min_env_per_group NULL Minimum environments representing each genetic group, where feasible.
balance_groups_across_env TRUE Balances group counts across environments.
force_group_connectivity TRUE Prioritises groups that have not reached min_env_per_group.
allow_approximate FALSE Relaxes exact equireplication only for an explicitly exploratory fallback.
seed NULL Reproducibility seed for allocation and tie-breaking.

5.1.3 Core tabular objects

Treatment information

treatment_info is required for family-guided allocation. It must contain one row per treatment and cover every allocated treatment.

Column Type Required Meaning
Treatment character yes Identifier matching treatments.
Family character yes for family grouping Breeding family or genetic stratum.
Additional columns any no Programme metadata retained outside the core allocator.

Example:

Treatment Family
G001 Fam01
G002 Fam01
G003 Fam07
Network-wide seed inventory

seed_info contains one row per treatment. SeedAvailable must be finite and non-negative. In seed-constrained workflows its unit is grams.

Column Type Required Meaning
Treatment character yes Identifier matching treatments.
SeedAvailable numeric yes Total inventory for the complete network, not inventory per site.

Example:

Treatment SeedAvailable
G001 185
G002 92
G003 240

Environment-specific seed requirement may be supplied as a scalar, a named numeric vector, or this data frame:

Environment SeedRequiredPerPlot
Environment_A 10
Environment_B 16
Environment_C 20

The allocation debit includes the mandatory local replication. For example, an alpha design with two replicates at Environment_C requires 2×20=402\times20=40 g for each treatment assigned there.

Treatment-to-matrix identifier map

id_map is needed only when field treatment IDs and relationship-matrix IDs differ.

Column Type Required Meaning
Treatment character yes Field and allocation identifier.
LineID character yes Corresponding row and column name in GRM or A.

Example:

Treatment LineID
G001 M001
G002 M002
G003 M003

5.1.4 Relationship and covariance matrices

A genomic relationship matrix (GRM) or pedigree numerator relationship matrix (A) uses treatment or mapped line IDs on both axes:

G001 G002 G003
G001 1.08 0.42 0.07
G002 0.42 1.03 0.05
G003 0.07 0.05 0.96

An environmental covariance matrix (Sigma_E) follows the same rule with environment IDs on both axes. Additive relationship is the default. A dominance matrix is optional and should be supplied only when hybrid or testcross dominance is part of the prediction target.

5.1.5 Local field-design specifications

env_design_specs is a named list, not a data frame. Each environment must use one of the two built-in engines.

For met_prep_famoptg, the required fields are design, check_treatments, check_families, n_blocks, n_rows, and n_cols. Optional pipeline fields include replication_mode, desired_replications, candidate_prep, max_prep, max_extra_replication_plots, shortage_action, and a named positive-integer vector fixed_treatment_reps.

For met_alpha_rc_stream, the required fields are design, check_treatments, check_families, n_reps, n_rows, and n_cols. Allocated entries and their families are inserted by the pipeline. Optional fields include min_block_size, max_block_size, cluster_source, order, serpentine, and seed.

All optional met_prep_famoptg specification fields are:

Field or fields Default Purpose
replication_mode Inferred Pipeline replication class: "augmented", "p_rep", or "rcbd_type".
desired_replications 2L Target plots for replicated entries.
candidate_prep NULL Entries eligible for partial replication.
max_prep NULL Maximum number of partially replicated entries.
max_extra_replication_plots NULL Physical ceiling on plots beyond one base plot per allocated entry.
shortage_action "downgrade" Seed-shortage response.
fixed_treatment_reps Empty named vector Exact site-specific replication for selected allocated entries.
order, serpentine "column", FALSE Field traversal direction and alternating traversal.
seed, attempts NULL, 1000 Randomisation seed and within-block search effort.
warn_and_correct, fix_rows TRUE, TRUE Whether and how an undersized grid is expanded.
cluster_source "Family" Adjacency groups from family, GRM, or A.
GRM, A, id_map NULL Conditional relationship inputs and identifier map.
cluster_method, cluster_seed, cluster_attempts, n_pcs_use "kmeans", 1, 25, Inf Relationship-based clustering controls.
check_placement, check_opt_attempts "random", 200 Random, systematic, or optimised check placement and its search effort.
use_dispersion, dispersion_source FALSE, "K" Optional local dispersion of related entries and the relationship source.
dispersion_radius, dispersion_iters, dispersion_seed 1, 2000, 1 Dispersion neighbourhood, search effort, and seed.
K, line_id_map NULL Conditional dispersion matrix and its identifier map.
verbose TRUE Print the local design summary.

All optional met_alpha_rc_stream specification fields are:

Field or fields Default Purpose
order, serpentine "column", FALSE Field traversal direction and alternating traversal.
seed, attempts NULL, 5000 Randomisation seed and within-block search effort.
warn_and_correct, fix_rows TRUE, TRUE Compatibility controls; alpha field geometry remains fixed.
cluster_source "Family" Adjacency groups from family, GRM, or A.
GRM, A, id_map NULL Conditional relationship inputs and identifier map.
cluster_method, cluster_seed, cluster_attempts, n_pcs_use "kmeans", 1, 25, Inf Relationship-based clustering controls.
n_blocks_per_rep NULL Exact incomplete-block count per replicate; otherwise inferred.
min_block_size, max_block_size NULL, NULL Bounds on total block size, including checks.
check_placement, check_position_pattern "systematic", "spread" Check-position controls.
use_dispersion, dispersion_source FALSE, "K" Optional local dispersion of related entries and the relationship source.
dispersion_radius, dispersion_iters, dispersion_seed 1, 2000, 1 Dispersion neighbourhood, search effort, and seed.
K, line_id_map NULL Conditional dispersion matrix and its identifier map.

env_design_specs <- list(
  Environment_A = list(
    design = "met_prep_famoptg",
    check_treatments = c("CHK_A", "CHK_B"),
    check_families = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
    n_blocks = 4L,
    n_rows = 12L,
    n_cols = 14L,
    replication_mode = "p_rep",
    desired_replications = 2L,
    max_extra_replication_plots = 36L
  ),

    check_treatments = c("CHK_A", "CHK_B"),

    n_reps = 2L,

    n_cols = 20L,

)

The physical grid must accommodate the fieldbook produced after check and replication plots are added. n_test_entries_per_environment is therefore not the same quantity as n_rows * n_cols.

5.1.6 Environmental evidence

Environmental inputs are optional for constructing a feasible fieldbook but required for environment-informed grouping, representativeness, or covariance analysis. Each feature block may be a data frame with an environment column or a matrix with environment row names.

Precomputed weather, soil, or management features
Column Type Required Meaning
environment character yes for data frames Environment identifier.
Feature columns numeric; management may also be categorical at least one Audited environmental variables or derived features.

Weather example:

environment T2M_mean_vegetative PRECTOTCORR_sum_reproductive VPD_q90
Environment_A 26.8 318.4 1.72
Environment_B 27.4 212.7 2.06
Environment_C 24.1 286.3 1.48

Management example:

environment planting_mode irrigation_mm nitrogen_kg_ha
Environment_A direct 420 130
Environment_B direct 510 145
Environment_C transplanting 620 160

Geography requires:

environment latitude longitude
Environment_A -1.80 -79.53
Environment_B 3.93 -75.02
Environment_C 3.50 -76.35
Historical MET values

Historical values are optional. When supplied, they must be adjusted genetic values or best linear unbiased estimates, not raw plot observations.

Column Type Required Meaning
genotype character yes Historical genotype identifier.
environment character yes Historical environment identifier.
value numeric yes Adjusted genetic value for the target trait.
year integer or character no Enables year-specific targets and leave-year-out validation.

Example:

genotype environment value year
H001 Environment_A 0.84 2023
H001 Environment_B 0.31 2023
H002 Environment_A -0.12 2023

Without valid historical MET values, Sigma_E is the identity matrix and the separate environmental kernels remain unweighted maximin scenarios.

5.1.7 Lower-level function requirements

When the pipeline functions are called separately:

  • allocate_sparse_met() requires treatments, environments, and n_test_entries_per_environment; allocation_method has a default.
  • assign_replication_by_seed() requires treatments, seed_available, and seed_required_per_plot; replication_mode defaults to "augmented".
  • met_prep_famoptg() requires checks, check families, the replicated and unreplicated treatment/family vectors, their replication counts, and block and field dimensions. Either non-check treatment set may be empty, but not both.
  • met_alpha_rc_stream() requires checks, check families, entry treatments, entry families, n_reps, n_rows, and n_cols.

The corresponding function help pages define every advanced optimiser and efficiency argument.

5.2 Minimum working example

The absolute minimum to run the full pipeline from allocation to field book:

library(OptiSparseMET)

# Minimum inputs: just lines, environments, and field dimensions
treatments <- paste0("L", sprintf("%03d", 1:120))
envs       <- c("E1", "E2", "E3", "E4")

# Stage 0: verify k
k <- suggest_safe_k(treatments, envs, buffer = 3)  # 33

# Stage 1: M3 allocation (no common treatments, no grouping)
alloc <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = treatments,
  environments                   = envs,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = k,
  seed                           = 1
)

# Stage 2: seed plan (uniform seed, no shortage)
seed_df <- data.frame(
  Treatment     = treatments,
  SeedAvailable = 100L
)
rep_plan <- assign_replication_by_seed(
  treatments             = treatments,
  seed_available         = seed_df,
  seed_required_per_plot = 10L,
  replication_mode       = "augmented"
)

# Stage 3: within-environment design (checks + unreplicated entries)
design <- met_prep_famoptg(
  check_treatments        = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families          = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  unreplicated_treatments = rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
  unreplicated_families   = rep("F1", length(rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments)),
  n_blocks = 4L, n_rows = 10L, n_cols = 12L,
  seed     = 1
)

# Stage 4: combine
met_book <- combine_met_fieldbooks(
  field_books = list(E1 = design$field_book)
)

6. Allocation Strategies

6.1 The random balanced strategy (M3)

The "random_balanced" method is a coverage-first stochastic allocation inspired by the M3 method of Montesinos-López et al. (2023). It operates in two phases:

Phase 1 (coverage guarantee): Every non-common line is assigned to at least one environment. Lines are processed in random order; each is placed in the environment with the most remaining capacity, with a preference for environments where the line’s genetic group is not yet represented when allocation_group_source is active.

Phase 2 (replication filling): Remaining slots are filled by repeatedly selecting lines with the largest replication deficit relative to target_replications, subject to group-balance penalties.

This strategy is appropriate when: - Environment capacities are heterogeneous - Exact balanced incomplete block design (BIBD) parameters are not achievable for the trial dimensions - Some flexibility in the incidence structure is acceptable

Unlike the original M3, which allocates environment by environment and may silently leave some lines with no assignment, this implementation guarantees full coverage before attempting any additional replication.

6.2 The balanced incomplete strategy (M4)

The "equireplicate" method implements the M4 allocation of Montesinos-López et al. (2023). It enforces two structural guarantees:

Condition 1 — Equal replication: every non-common line appears in exactly rr environments. This ensures no line is systematically under-evaluated and is the defining property that distinguishes M4 from M3. Here, replication means distinct-environment incidence, not repeated plots within a location. Local plot replication never increases cross-environment connectivity.

Condition 2 — Exact requested environment sizes: environment ee receives its requested ke*k_e^* sparse lines. Loads may differ, provided ∑eke*=J*r\sum_e k_e^* = J^*r and the equal-replication degree sequence is realisable. The familiar J*r=Ik*J^*r = Ik^* identity is the equal-size special case.

These two conditions are what matter in plant breeding programmes where thousands of candidate lines are tested across a few environments. Enforcing them means every line gets the same number of chances to be evaluated — a fundamental fairness and precision requirement.

For novice readers: Equal replication means that if two breeders each select the “top 10% of lines” based on the trial data, they are working from the same quality of information for every line. Without equal replication, lines tested more often have lower-variance estimates and a systematic advantage in selection.

allow_approximate = FALSE (the default) enforces both conditions strictly. The total slot identity and Gale-Ryser degree condition must hold, and the function stops clearly otherwise. Use check_equireplicate_feasibility() before allocating. The equal-capacity example below reduces to the classic identity:

# With k=39, J*=112, I=4, r=1: available slots = 4*(39-8) = 124,
# required slots = 112*1 = 112. 124 ≠ 112 -> slot identity fails.
check_balanced_incomplete_feasibility(
  n_treatments_total             = 120,
  n_environments                 = 4,
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 39,
  target_replications            = 1,
  n_common_treatments            = 8
)
# feasible   = FALSE  (available = 124, required = 112, difference = 12)
# Adjust k so that J*×r = I×k*: e.g. k=36 -> k*=28, 4*28=112=112*1.

# With k=36: slot identity holds.
check_balanced_incomplete_feasibility(
  n_treatments_total             = 120,
  n_environments                 = 4,
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 36,
  target_replications            = 1,
  n_common_treatments            = 8
)
# feasible = TRUE (difference = 0)

Construction uses a greedy load-balanced constructor that guarantees equal replication.

allow_approximate = TRUE relaxes the slot identity and accepts minor replication imbalances. This is a fallback for exploratory use when exact slot identity cannot be achieved, not the primary path.

6.3 M3 versus M4: choosing the right strategy

Feature M3 "random_balanced" M4 "equireplicate"
Equal replication guarantee No (approximate) Yes (allow_approximate = FALSE)
Exact requested environment sizes Yes Yes when the degree sequence is realisable
Pairwise co-occurrence Stochastic Approximately uniform; compute from $allocation_matrix %*% t($allocation_matrix)
Handles unequal environment sizes Yes Yes, including strict mode
Requires total identity ∑eke*=J*r\sum_e k_e^* = J^*r No Yes (strict mode)
Coverage guarantee Yes (phase 1) Yes
Typical use Heterogeneous programmes, exploratory Standard MET networks with equal replication

In practice, M3 is more flexible and tolerates heterogeneous constraints. M4 with allow_approximate = FALSE (the default) is the correct choice whenever equal replication is a hard requirement — which it should be in most standard breeding programmes. Verify the total slot identity and degree sequence first with check_equireplicate_feasibility() and adjust the site loads or rr when needed. M4 with allow_approximate = TRUE is a fallback when strict equal replication cannot be satisfied.

library(OptiSparseMET)

data("OptiSparseMET_example_data")
x <- OptiSparseMET_example_data

# Verify feasibility first
suggest_safe_k(x$treatments, x$environments,
               common_treatments = x$common_treatments, buffer = 3)
# Returns 39: ceil(112/4) + 8 + 3 = 39

# M3: random balanced allocation
alloc_M3 <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 39,
  target_replications            = 1,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments,
  seed                           = 123
)

# M4: balanced incomplete allocation with equal replication.
# J*=112, I=4, r=1: need k* = 112/4 = 28, k = 28+8 = 36.
# Slot identity: 112*1 = 4*28 = 112. Verified above.
alloc_M4 <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  allocation_method              = "equireplicate",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 36,
  target_replications            = 1,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments,
  allow_approximate              = FALSE,
  seed                           = 123
)

alloc_M3$summary  # allocation_method, min/max/mean replication, etc.
alloc_M4$summary  # min_sparse_replication = max_sparse_replication = 1 (equal)
alloc_M4$summary$max_sparse_replication  # equals min_sparse_replication: equal replication confirmed

6.4 Equal-size special case: divisibility by J*, I, and r

For equal environment sizes, J*×r=I×k*J^* \times r = I \times k^* requires that J*×rJ^* \times r be exactly divisible by II. Whether this is achievable for a given combination of sparse treatments (J*J^*), environments (II), and replication (rr) depends on the shared factors of these three numbers.

The divisibility rule

For the slot identity to hold, II must divide J*×rJ^* \times r exactly. Every prime factor of II that is absent from J*J^* must be supplied by rr. This has a practical consequence for the most common case in plant breeding:

  • I=4I = 4 environments, J*J^* odd: J*×1=oddJ^* \times 1 = \text{odd} (not divisible by 4); J*×2=2×oddJ^* \times 2 = 2 \times \text{odd} (divisible by 2 but not by 4 for odd J*J^*); only r=4r = 4 guarantees divisibility. But r=4r = 4 gives k*=J*k^* = J^* — full replication — which defeats the purpose of sparse testing. Practical fix: adjust CC by 1 so that J*=J−CJ^* = J - C becomes even.

  • I=4I = 4 environments, J*J^* even but not divisible by 4: r=2r = 2 always works (e.g. J*=110J^* = 110: 110×2/4=55110 \times 2 / 4 = 55).

  • I=3I = 3 environments: feasibility depends on divisibility by 3. If J*J^* is divisible by 3, any rr works. Otherwise rr must be a multiple of 3.

  • I=6I = 6 environments: requires divisibility by 2×3=62 \times 3 = 6. Odd J*J^* not divisible by 3 requires rr divisible by 6.

Feasibility table: r=2r = 2

The table shows k*k^* when the slot identity holds, and -- when it does not for that combination. Add CC (common treatments) to k*k^* to get the n_test_entries_per_environment argument.
