What to do when your combination gives --

Use check_equireplicate_feasibility() to diagnose the problem and try one of these adjustments:

  1. Adjust CC by 1: adding or removing one common treatment changes J*J^* by 1, which may make it divisible by II for the chosen rr.
  2. Try r=2r = 2 instead of r=1r = 1, or r=3r = 3 instead of r=2r = 2 — the extra factor may resolve the divisibility.
  3. Use random_balanced (M3) if exact equal replication is not essential. M3 does not require the slot identity and tolerates odd J*J^* freely.
  4. Use allow_approximate = TRUE as a fallback — the allocation proceeds with the closest possible balance, accepting minor replication differences.
# Quick check: is your combination feasible?
# J* = 75 (odd), I = 4, r = 2 -- should give --
check_balanced_incomplete_feasibility(
  n_treatments_total             = 83,   # J = J* + C = 75 + 8
  n_environments                 = 4,
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 30,   # k* guess: 30 - 8 = 22, 4*22=88 != 75*2=150
  target_replications            = 2,
  n_common_treatments            = 8
)
# feasible = FALSE -> adjust

# Fix: change C from 8 to 9 -> J* = 74 (even), r=2: 74*2/4 = 37
check_balanced_incomplete_feasibility(
  n_treatments_total             = 83,
  n_environments                 = 4,
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 46,   # k* = 37, k = 37+9 = 46
  target_replications            = 2,
  n_common_treatments            = 9
)
# feasible = TRUE

7. Genetic Structure-Aware Allocation

Standard allocation treats lines as exchangeable — any line could go to any environment with equal probability. This is inadequate when:

  • Genomic prediction is a downstream objective (related lines clustered in the same environments provide redundant rather than complementary information)
  • Family structure is strong and environments differ in their genetic composition
  • Genetic disconnectedness would bias G×E estimation

OptiSparseMET incorporates genetic structure through three mechanisms, controlled by allocation_group_source in allocate_sparse_met().

7.1 Family-based allocation ("Family")

Family labels (e.g., full-sib or half-sib families) are read from treatment_info$Family. Lines from the same family are treated as a group and the allocator distributes groups across environments rather than concentrating them. This prevents any one environment from containing a disproportionate fraction of one family’s members, which would inflate within-family variance estimates and reduce the effective diversity of each site’s test set.

7.2 GRM-based allocation ("GRM")

When marker data are available, the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) encodes pairwise genetic similarity between all candidate lines. The allocator performs principal component analysis (PCA) on the GRM, then clusters lines by their positions in genomic principal component space using k-means or hierarchical clustering. The resulting cluster labels guide allocation just as family labels do.

This approach is more precise than family-based allocation when families are heterogeneous in size or when marker data captures structure not visible from pedigree labels alone. It directly improves the conditions under which genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) models operate by ensuring that genomically similar lines are spread across environments.

7.3 Pedigree-based allocation ("A")

When genomic data are unavailable, the pedigree numerator relationship matrix AA plays the same role as the GRM. PCA is performed on AA and clustering proceeds identically. The resulting groups reflect pedigree relatedness rather than marker-estimated genomic similarity.

7.4 Why this matters for prediction

Under a GBLUP model, prediction accuracy for unobserved lines depends on their relatedness to observed lines. When genetically similar lines are clustered in the same environments, the model gets redundant replication of the same genetic profiles while other profiles go unobserved. Spreading related lines across environments ensures the full genetic diversity of the candidate set is represented at each site, maximizing the amount of novel genetic information available for calibrating the prediction model.

alloc_grm <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 39,
  target_replications            = 1,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments,
  allocation_group_source        = "GRM",
  GRM                            = x$OptiSparseMET_GRM,
  treatment_info                 = x$treatment_info,
  group_method                   = "kmeans",
  group_seed                     = 42,
  group_attempts                 = 25,
  min_groups_per_environment     = 4,
  min_env_per_group              = 2,
  balance_groups_across_env      = TRUE,
  force_group_connectivity       = TRUE,
  seed                           = 123
)

alloc_grm$group_by_environment  # how many lines per group per environment
alloc_grm$group_overlap_matrix  # how many groups are shared across env pairs

7.5 From environmental observations to Sigma_E

An environmental relationship is a description of sites; it is not, by itself, an estimate of genetic covariance. The recommended workflow therefore keeps the sources separate:

dedicated_interaction_hypotheses <- data.frame(
  interaction = c(
    "temperature_x_density", "temperature_x_density"
  ),
  parent = c("temperature", "density"),
  modality = c("weather", "soil"),
  variable = c("T2M_mean_reproductive", "bulk_density_root")
)

kb <- build_environment_kernels(
  weather = historical_weather_features,
  soil = root_zone_soil_features,
  management = planned_management,
  geography = site_coordinates,
  bandwidth_multipliers = c(0.5, 1, 2),
  include_interactions = TRUE,
  variable_interactions = dedicated_interaction_hypotheses
)

variable_evidence <- assess_variable_interactions(
  kb$kernels,
  historical = adjusted_historical_MET_values,
  year_col = "year",
  p_adjust = "holm",
  n_boot = 500,
  seed = 2026
)

ec <- calibrate_environment_covariance(
  kb$kernels,
  historical = adjusted_historical_MET_values,
  year_col = "year",
  eligible_interactions = variable_evidence$supported,
  ridge = 0
)
Sigma_E <- ec$Sigma_E
ec$status
ec$cross_validation

include_interactions = TRUE constructs all available pairwise weather-by-soil, weather-by-management, and soil-by-management kernels. The default is a centred functional analysis of variance (functional-ANOVA) construction, (HKaH)∘(HKbH)(H K_a H)\circ(H K_b H), which represents joint deviations after removing the constant feature-space baseline from each parent. This is preferable to the legacy raw product because it reduces main-effect leakage. Explicit higher-order hypotheses can be supplied with interaction_terms, while interaction_mode = "product" remains available for reproducibility with older analyses. These are candidate covariance structures—not evidence that a biological interaction exists. Historical MET responses must support their contribution through a paired blocked-validation comparison against a main-effects-only model. Unsupported interaction weights are fixed at zero. Every interaction kernel remains a separate structural uncertainty scenario, including when its central weight is zero or cannot be estimated. Without historical responses, interactions never enter the central covariance, but they are evaluated without weights through maximin robust design. This avoids equating absence of response evidence with absence of a physical interaction. The production workflow propagates that same uncertainty set through capacity selection, common-treatment optimisation, allocation refinement, and final robust evaluation. Across-year weather analysis also retains the most atypical observed-year weather-by-soil and weather-by-management structures.

The package distinguishes omnibus modality interactions from dedicated variable interactions. A Gaussian weather kernel represents nonlinear functions and interactions among all weather variables implicitly. Similarly, weather_x_soil contains the full weather-by-soil tensor-product hypothesis. Neither object isolates a named combination. Therefore, variable_interactions should be used when a hypothesis such as reproductive temperature by root-zone bulk density must be guaranteed and audited separately.

The recommended input is a long data frame:

Column Type Required Meaning
interaction character yes Unique hypothesis label
parent character yes Parent label within that hypothesis
modality character yes Covariate-block name
variable character yes Exact post-quality-control variable name

For example:

interaction parent modality variable
temperature_x_density temperature weather T2M_mean_reproductive
temperature_x_density density soil bulk_density_root
rainfall_x_clay rainfall weather PRECTOTCORR_sum_reproductive
rainfall_x_clay clay soil clay_root

Each named interaction is constructed from the row-wise tensor product of its standardised parent variables. By default, the tensor features are residualised against the intercept and all parent main effects before the Gaussian bandwidth-ensemble kernel is built. Strong heredity retains the exact parent-variable kernels. The returned variable_interaction_audit, variable_ledger, and kernel_hierarchy document the matched variables, tensor dimensions, residual information, effective rank, realised bandwidths, and parent-child relationships.

assess_variable_interactions() compares each dedicated interaction with the same main-effect model. Leave-year-out validation is preferred when year-specific historical targets exist; otherwise leave-environment-out validation is used. Holm correction controls multiplicity. Positive mean prediction improvement, an adjusted paired sign test below the declared threshold, and a positive covariance contribution are all required before an interaction becomes eligible for the central covariance. Bootstrap inclusion quantifies stability. Screened interactions remain separate structural uncertainty scenarios.

If historical adjusted genetic values are unavailable, no interaction is labelled supported or unsupported. assess_variable_interactions() returns decision = "structural_uncertainty", while calibrate_environment_covariance() retains identity as the central covariance and returns every broad and dedicated kernel as an unweighted maximin candidate. Hence, a physical hypothesis is represented without being converted into arbitrary genetic covariance.

Each source passes through qc_environmental_data(), which returns explicit coverage, range, provenance, and imputation ledgers. The separate-kernel construction means a 150-column weather block does not receive fifteen times the weight of a ten-column soil block. Gaussian bandwidth sensitivity is integrated within each modality. Modalities are combined as genetic covariance only when historical MET values support estimation of their weights.

For rice, rice_weather_features() supports actual phenological stages or thermal time and derives vapour-pressure deficit (VPD), precipitation-minus-evapotranspiration (P-ET) balance, hot nights, heat/cold severity, root water deficit, and consecutive stress spells. fetch_soilgrids() can retrieve several depths and Q0.05/Q0.5/Q0.95 predictions; soil_profile_features() produces thickness-weighted root-zone summaries, uncertainty widths, available water, neighbourhood heterogeneity, and compositional texture coordinates.

If historical adjusted genetic values are unavailable, calibrate_environment_covariance() returns status = "no_historical_met", weights = NULL, and identity as the central Sigma_E. Every modality kernel and every interaction kernel is retained separately as a sensitivity structure for robust_scenarios(Sigma_E_candidates = ...); no arbitrary mixture is formed. For descriptive mega-environment clustering, consensus_environment_kernels() combines within-kernel ranks by their median, without elicited weights. This descriptive consensus must not be called genetic covariance. Use maximin aggregation across the separate structures when no MET evidence is available, rather than assigning them arbitrary scenario probabilities. The same maximin rule is retained when historical calibration exists because rejected or weakly identified interaction structures still lack defensible probabilities. Across-year weather consensus is computed within the weather modality only, so instability in weather never removes soil, management, or geography.

The number of descriptive groups should normally be estimated with infer_mega_environments(), not supplied beforehand. It compares hierarchical clustering and k-means on kernel principal coordinates over every feasible group count. K-means uses finite objective descent from multiple non-empty starts, guaranteeing termination without an iteration-limit failure. Minimum group size and silhouette separation screen out weak solutions; adjusted-Rand agreement across methods, modalities, years, and relationship-level bootstrap consensuses screens out unstable solutions. Years can be assigned to a common evidence block with relationship_groups, preventing a long weather archive from acting as an implicit weather weight. No weighted index chooses the winning number of groups. If none passes all requirements, the result is an explicitly unpartitioned network. With only one evidence block any accepted result is labelled provisional, and hard genetic mega-environment claims still require historical MET response evidence.

8. Common Treatments

Common treatments are lines assigned to every environment before sparse allocation begins. If CC is the number of common treatments, each environment has its effective sparse capacity reduced:

ke*=ke−Ck_e^* = k_e - C

and the number of sparse-allocatable lines is:

J*=J−CJ^* = J - C

8.1 Why common treatments matter

Common treatments serve two statistically distinct purposes.

Design-based connectivity: Two environments that share no tested lines can only be linked through the model — through the assumed structure of KK. Common treatments provide direct comparisons that do not depend on any model assumption. This is important when environments are weakly genetically correlated or when the researcher wants robust cross-site inference.

Estimation stability: Common treatments appear in every environment, so their effects are estimated with the highest precision. They function as stable benchmarks against which the performance of sparse treatments is measured. In practice, they are often elite lines or standard checks whose behaviour is already partially known.

For novice readers: Common treatments are like reference points in a measurement system. Even if two environments test completely different sets of experimental lines, they can still be compared through their shared reference lines — just as two labs can compare results if they all measure the same control sample.

8.2 What is selected during planning and fixed after selection

The package does not impose one universal common-set size. This does not mean that common-genotype identities remain changeable after a design is released. Two planning routes are available:

  1. If biological, operational, or external evidence has already identified the anchors, supply those identities through common_treatments. Allocation treats the supplied set as fixed and places every member in every environment.
  2. If the set has not been chosen, suggest_common_treatments() provides a feasible starting point and optimize_common_treatments() compares nested sizes and candidate identities. The optimizer chooses a larger set only when its gain in robust information justifies the loss of sparse testing breadth.

Once an optimized result is accepted and passed to allocation, its membership is fixed in exactly the same way as a user-supplied set. Re-running the planning analysis with changed evidence, capacities, seed inventory, or uncertainty scenarios can produce a different proposal; the released fieldbook does not adapt or change by itself.

More common treatments strengthen direct connectivity and can improve precision, but they also consume plots and seed that would otherwise increase testing breadth. The planning decision is therefore made jointly with genotype identity. Local plot replication is deliberately decided later.

8.3 Robust common-set selection and separate local replication

Presence and replication are different decisions. A treatment is common when its presence is fixed at every environment in the selected design; it may have one plot at one site, two at another, and more at a third when the local design and seed inventory permit. For production planning, optimize_common_treatments() compares nested common sets across residual-variance and Sigma_E uncertainty scenarios. Its criterion combines robust TPE reliability, pairwise environment connectivity, genetic effective sample size, and retained testing breadth. Family/group coverage, full-population coverage, entry capacities, and the network-wide seed needed for one presence plot at every environment are hard constraints.

Pairwise correlation differences affect the effective shared-treatment target for every environment pair. pair_aggregate = "maximin" is the default and protects the least-connected pair. "cvar" protects the weakest lower tail, whereas "mean" maximises average pairwise attainment. These are pairwise scoring rules for one global common set. Repeating a genotype at one or both sites does not increase the shared-treatment count. Genetic effective sample size evaluates diversity separately; it does not replace the literal number of distinct shared identities.

common_opt <- optimize_common_treatments(
  G = G, Sigma_E = Sigma_E,
  treatment_info = treatment_info,
  seed_info = seed_info,
  # Multiply per-plot seed by any mandatory local plot count first.
  seed_required_per_plot = mandatory_seed_per_presence,
  entry_capacities = site_entries,
  minimum_seed_buffer = 0,
  aggregate = "cvar",
  pair_aggregate = "maximin"
)

common_opt$common_presence
common_opt$pareto

common_presence is binary and records the chosen global core. Pass common_opt$selected to allocation. Local one-, two-, or higher-plot replication is then assigned by plan_sparse_met_design() or assign_replication_by_seed() from the seed remaining after network allocation.

Connectivity itself is evaluated from distinct shared genotypes in the binary allocation matrix. A genotype contributes one shared treatment to an environment pair whether it has one plot or several at either site. Supplying Sigma_E to allocate_sparse_met() or plan_sparse_met_design() activates correlation-adaptive, margin-preserving swaps: weakly connected pairs can receive more distinct shared sparse treatments, whereas strongly connected pairs may require fewer. Plot replication remains a downstream seed-feasible precision decision.

9. Seed-Aware Replication

9.1 The feasibility constraint

A design that requests replication without accounting for available seed cannot be deployed. Across a network, the same inventory must not be reset at every site. A genotype consumes zero seed at any site where it is absent; where it is present, its consumption is accumulated across all delivered plots. The joint feasibility condition for genotype ii is:

si≥∑erieqe+bs_i \geq \sum_e r_{ie}q_e + b

where: - sis_i = seed available for genotype ii, in grams - rier_{ie} = delivered plots in environment ee - qeq_e = grams required per plot in environment ee - bb = optional reserve in grams

The default reserve is 0 g. A positive value should be supplied only when the breeding programme has an explicit retention, germination, or replanting policy; it is not imposed as a statistical requirement.

9.2 Replication roles

plan_sparse_met_design() enforces the joint condition during allocation and local replication, then reconstructs a final seed_ledger from all fieldbooks. For a single local environment, assign_replication_by_seed() evaluates the corresponding one-site condition and assigns one of three roles:

  • "p_rep" — sufficient seed for rir_i plots; assigned desired_replications plots
  • "unreplicated" — sufficient seed for one plot but not for desired_replications plots (downgraded)
  • "excluded" — insufficient seed even for one plot

Three design modes control how these roles are assigned:

Mode "augmented" "p_rep" "rcbd_type"
Target 1 plot per line rr plots for a feasible subset rr plots for all lines
Downgrade Excluded if seed < qeq_e Non-candidates get 1 plot Yes, if shortage_action = "downgrade"
P-rep selection — By priority (seed, order, random) — 
seed_df <- data.frame(
  Treatment     = x$treatments,
  SeedAvailable = sample(20:120, length(x$treatments), replace = TRUE)
)

rep_plan <- assign_replication_by_seed(
  treatments             = x$treatments,
  seed_available         = seed_df,
  seed_required_per_plot = 10,
  replication_mode       = "p_rep",
  desired_replications   = 2,
  priority               = "seed_available",
  max_prep               = 20,
  minimum_seed_buffer    = 5,
  shortage_action        = "downgrade",
  seed                   = 123
)

length(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments)        # replicated at 2 reps
length(rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments) # assigned 1 plot (downgraded)
length(rep_plan$excluded_treatments)     # insufficient seed
rep_plan$seed_summary                    # full per-line feasibility table

10. Within-Environment Design Engines

10.1 met_prep_famoptg() — block-based repeated-check designs

This engine constructs repeated-check block designs for environments where the primary local control mechanism is blocking (incomplete block designs). It supports three design classes:

Augmented repeated-check design

All non-check lines are unreplicated. Each block contains the same set of check treatments plus a unique subset of experimental lines. This design is appropriate for early screening stages when the number of candidates far exceeds available resources and seed is very limited. The checks allow estimation of block effects, which are subtracted to improve comparisons among the unreplicated lines.

Partially replicated (p-rep) design

A subset of lines — those with more seed or higher priority — is replicated at desired_replications plots, distributed across distinct blocks. The remainder appear unreplicated. P-rep designs are efficient because they concentrate replication where it provides the most information while still including a broad set of candidates.

RCBD-type repeated-check design

All non-check lines are replicated at a uniform level. This is the closest to a standard RCBD within a single environment, extended to include repeated checks in every block.

Structural guarantees enforced by met_prep_famoptg():

  • Check treatments appear in every block
  • Replicated lines appear in distinct blocks (at most once per block)
  • Unreplicated lines appear exactly once in the design

Optional features include family-based or GRM/A-based genetic dispersion optimisation (minimising the average relatedness of adjacent plots) and mixed-model efficiency evaluation (A, D, CDmean).

design_E1 <- met_prep_famoptg(
  check_treatments        = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families          = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  p_rep_treatments        = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  p_rep_reps              = rep_plan$p_rep_reps,
  p_rep_families          = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  unreplicated_treatments = rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
  unreplicated_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_blocks     = 4L,
  n_rows       = 10L,
  n_cols       = 12L,
  order        = "row",
  serpentine   = TRUE,
  seed         = 123
)

design_E1$layout_matrix  # plot-level field map
design_E1$field_book     # row-level data frame ready for export

10.2 met_alpha_rc_stream() — row-column alpha designs

This engine constructs alpha row-column designs for large fields where both row and column gradients are present. It is most appropriate when:

  • The field is large and rectangular
  • Row and column variation is substantial relative to treatment differences
  • A first-order autoregressive spatial residual model in one dimension (AR1) or two dimensions (AR1×AR1) will be used at analysis

The design is built by streaming plots across the field in a specified traversal order (row-major, column-major, or serpentine). Each replicate occupies a contiguous block of rows or columns. Within each replicate, entries are partitioned into incomplete blocks, with check treatments inserted at regular intervals within every incomplete block.

Structural guarantees:

  • Each entry appears exactly once per replicate
  • Check treatments appear in every incomplete block
  • Block sizes are constrained within [min_block_size, max_block_size] 
design_E2 <- met_alpha_rc_stream(
  check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families   = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  entry_treatments = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  entry_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                       match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                             x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_reps         = 2L,
  n_rows         = 10L,
  n_cols         = 12L,
  min_block_size = 8L,
  max_block_size = 12L,
  order          = "row",
  serpentine     = TRUE,
  seed           = 123
)

design_E2$layout_matrix
design_E2$field_book
design_E2$design_info   # n_reps, n_blocks_per_rep, total_used_plots

10.3 Design engine selection guide

Use met_prep_famoptg() when:

  • Repeated check distribution across blocks is a structural requirement
  • The design needs to support p-rep, augmented, or RCBD-type structure
  • The field is subdivided into blocks but row-column spatial modelling is not the primary concern

Use met_alpha_rc_stream() when:

  • The field is large and continuous, with both row and column gradients
  • Spatial models (AR1 or AR1×AR1) will be used at analysis
  • The design needs fixed-grid compatibility for automated plot management

The engines can be mixed across environments within the same trial.

11. Efficiency Evaluation

11.1 Block-based designs: met_evaluate_famoptg_efficiency()

For designs produced by met_prep_famoptg(), efficiency is evaluated under a model with a block random effect:

y=Xβ+Zg+Wb+ey = X\beta + Zg + Wb + e

where b∼N(0,Iσb2)b \sim N(0,\, I\sigma_b^2) is the block effect. The variance components are specified in varcomp using sigma_b2 for the block variance. Note that this model has a single block variance component — there is no separate replicate or incomplete-block-within-replicate structure.

The function computes A-criterion, D-criterion (for fixed treatment effects), and CDmean (for random treatment effects), under any of three residual structures: "IID", "AR1" (along rows or columns), or "AR1xAR1" (spatial gradient in both dimensions).

eff_E1 <- met_evaluate_famoptg_efficiency(
  field_book       = design_E1$field_book,
  n_rows           = 10L,
  n_cols           = 12L,
  check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  varcomp = list(
    sigma_e2  = 1.0,   # residual variance
    sigma_g2  = 0.5,   # genetic variance (for CDmean)
    sigma_b2  = 0.3,   # block variance
    sigma_r2  = 0.05,  # row variance (for spatial structures)
    sigma_c2  = 0.05   # column variance
  ),
  treatment_effect    = "random",
  prediction_type     = "IID",
  residual_structure  = "IID"
)

eff_E1$CDmean     # in [0, 1]: higher is better
eff_E1$mean_PEV   # mean prediction error variance
eff_E1$A          # A-efficiency (1 / A_criterion): higher is better
eff_E1$D          # D-efficiency: higher is better

11.2 Row-column designs: met_evaluate_alpha_efficiency()

For designs produced by met_alpha_rc_stream(), efficiency is evaluated under a model with replicate and incomplete-block-within-replicate random effects:

y=Xβ+Zg+Wrr+Wbb+ey = X\beta + Zg + W_r r + W_{b} b + e

where r∼N(0,Iσrep2)r \sim N(0,\, I\sigma_{\text{rep}}^2) and b∼N(0,Iσib2)b \sim N(0,\, I\sigma_{\text{ib}}^2) are the replicate and incomplete block effects respectively. The varcomp list must contain sigma_rep2 and sigma_ib2 (not sigma_b2). This two-level blocking structure reflects the hierarchical design of alpha row-column layouts.

eff_E2 <- met_evaluate_alpha_efficiency(
  field_book       = design_E2$field_book,
  n_rows           = 10L,
  n_cols           = 12L,
  check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  varcomp = list(
    sigma_e2   = 1.0,
    sigma_g2   = 0.5,
    sigma_rep2 = 0.4,   # replicate variance
    sigma_ib2  = 0.2,   # incomplete block within replicate
    sigma_r2   = 0.05,
    sigma_c2   = 0.05
  ),
  treatment_effect   = "random",
  prediction_type    = "IID",
  residual_structure = "IID"
)

eff_E2$CDmean
eff_E2$mean_PEV

Key distinction: met_evaluate_famoptg_efficiency() uses sigma_b2 (one block level); met_evaluate_alpha_efficiency() uses sigma_rep2 + sigma_ib2 (two block levels: replicate and incomplete block within replicate). Using the wrong function for the wrong design will produce an error or incorrect results.

12. Design Optimisation

Once a base design is constructed and its efficiency evaluated, the optimizer functions search for a better arrangement of the same treatments within the same blocking structure.

12.1 met_optimize_famoptg() — block-based optimisation

met_optimize_famoptg() uses Random Restart (RS): it generates multiple independent random designs, evaluates each, and returns the best. All structural guarantees of met_prep_famoptg() are enforced in every candidate design.

opt_E1 <- met_optimize_famoptg(
  # All arguments of met_prep_famoptg(), plus:
  check_treatments        = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families          = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  p_rep_treatments        = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  p_rep_reps              = rep_plan$p_rep_reps,
  p_rep_families          = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  unreplicated_treatments = rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
  unreplicated_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_blocks            = 4L,
  n_rows              = 10L,
  n_cols              = 12L,
  # Optimisation arguments:
  treatment_effect    = "random",
  prediction_type     = "IID",
  criterion           = "CDmean",
  varcomp = list(sigma_e2=1, sigma_g2=0.5, sigma_b2=0.3,
                 sigma_r2=0.05, sigma_c2=0.05),
  n_restarts          = 20L,
  seed                = 123
)

opt_E1$optimization$best_score    # best CDmean found
opt_E1$optimization$score_history # CDmean at each restart
opt_E1$optimization$n_failed      # restarts that produced invalid designs
opt_E1$field_book                 # the best design's field book
opt_E1$efficiency                 # efficiency metrics of the best design

12.2 met_optimize_alpha_rc() — row-column optimisation

met_optimize_alpha_rc() supports three optimisation algorithms:

RS (Random Restart): Same as met_optimize_famoptg(). Generates multiple independent candidates and keeps the best. Simple and parallelizable.

SA (Simulated Annealing): Starts from one design and iteratively perturbs it. At each step, a worse design is accepted with probability exp⁡(−Δ/T)\exp(-\Delta / T), where Δ\Delta is the score decrease and TT is the current temperature. As TT decreases from sa_temp_start to sa_temp_end, the algorithm transitions from broad exploration to local refinement. SA is effective when the fitness landscape has many local optima.

GA (Genetic Algorithm): Maintains a population of designs. At each generation, pairs of high-scoring designs are combined (“crossover”) and random perturbations are applied (“mutation”). Elite designs are carried forward unchanged. GA explores a broader search space than RS or SA for the same number of objective function evaluations, at the cost of higher implementation complexity.

# Simulated Annealing
opt_E2_sa <- met_optimize_alpha_rc(
  check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families   = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  entry_treatments = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  entry_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                       match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                             x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_reps            = 2L,
  n_rows            = 10L,
  n_cols            = 12L,
  method            = "SA",
  treatment_effect  = "random",
  prediction_type   = "IID",
  criterion         = "CDmean",
  varcomp = list(sigma_e2=1, sigma_g2=0.5, sigma_rep2=0.4,
                 sigma_ib2=0.2, sigma_r2=0.05, sigma_c2=0.05),
  sa_max_iter       = 500L,
  sa_temp_start     = 1.0,
  sa_temp_end       = 0.01,
  seed              = 123
)

opt_E2_sa$optimization$best_score
opt_E2_sa$optimization$sa_params   # SA-specific settings
opt_E2_sa$optimization$ga_params   # NULL (not used)

# Genetic Algorithm
opt_E2_ga <- met_optimize_alpha_rc(
  check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
  check_families   = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
  entry_treatments = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  entry_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                       match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                             x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_reps            = 2L,
  n_rows            = 10L,
  n_cols            = 12L,
  method            = "GA",
  treatment_effect  = "random",
  prediction_type   = "IID",
  criterion         = "CDmean",
  varcomp = list(sigma_e2=1, sigma_g2=0.5, sigma_rep2=0.4,
                 sigma_ib2=0.2, sigma_r2=0.05, sigma_c2=0.05),
  ga_pop_size       = 20L,
  ga_n_generations  = 50L,
  ga_elitism        = 4L,
  seed              = 123
)

opt_E2_ga$optimization$best_score
opt_E2_ga$optimization$ga_params

13. Full Pipeline Example

13.1 Step-by-step 

library(OptiSparseMET)

data("OptiSparseMET_example_data")
x <- OptiSparseMET_example_data

# Stage 0: verify capacity
k_safe <- suggest_safe_k(x$treatments, x$environments,
                         common_treatments = x$common_treatments,
                         buffer = 3)   # 39

# Stage 1: allocation
# k_safe = 39 does not satisfy the slot identity for M4 (112*1=112 ≠ 4*31=124).
# Use random_balanced (M3) here, or adjust k for M4 slot identity.
# For M4 with r=1: k* = 112/4 = 28, k = 36.
alloc <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = k_safe,
  target_replications            = 1,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments,
  allocation_group_source        = "Family",
  treatment_info                 = x$treatment_info,
  seed                           = 123
)

alloc$summary
alloc$overlap_matrix   # environments x environments: how many lines shared

# Stage 2: seed-aware replication
rep_plan <- assign_replication_by_seed(
  treatments             = x$treatments,
  seed_available         = x$seed_info,
  seed_required_per_plot = 8,
  replication_mode       = "p_rep",
  desired_replications   = 2,
  max_prep               = 15,
  shortage_action        = "downgrade",
  seed                   = 123
)

# Stage 3: design per environment (example for Env_A)
design_A <- met_prep_famoptg(
  check_treatments        = x$env_design_specs$Env_A$check_treatments,
  check_families          = x$env_design_specs$Env_A$check_families,
  p_rep_treatments        = rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
  p_rep_reps              = rep_plan$p_rep_reps,
  p_rep_families          = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$p_rep_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  unreplicated_treatments = rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
  unreplicated_families   = x$treatment_info$Family[
                              match(rep_plan$unreplicated_treatments,
                                    x$treatment_info$Treatment)],
  n_blocks   = x$env_design_specs$Env_A$n_blocks,
  n_rows     = x$env_design_specs$Env_A$n_rows,
  n_cols     = x$env_design_specs$Env_A$n_cols,
  seed       = 123
)

# Stage 4: combine field books
met_book <- combine_met_fieldbooks(
  field_books       = list(Env_A = design_A$field_book),
  local_designs     = c(Env_A = "met_prep_famoptg"),
  replication_modes = c(Env_A = "p_rep"),
  sparse_method     = "equireplicate",
  common_treatments = x$common_treatments
)

head(met_book)

13.2 End-to-end pipeline

plan_sparse_met_design() executes all four stages in a single call. Each environment’s local design is controlled by env_design_specs, a named list where the design field specifies "met_prep_famoptg" or "met_alpha_rc_stream":

out <- plan_sparse_met_design(
  treatments                     = x$treatments,
  environments                   = x$environments,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 39,
  target_replications            = 1,
  common_treatments              = x$common_treatments,
  env_design_specs               = x$env_design_specs,
  treatment_info                 = x$treatment_info,
  seed_info                      = x$seed_info,
  seed_required_per_plot         = x$seed_required_per_plot,
  minimum_seed_buffer            = 1,
  seed                           = 123
)

names(out)
# "sparse_allocation"    "environment_designs"   "combined_field_book"
# "environment_summary"  "group_environment_summary"
# "efficiency_summary"   "seed_ledger"  "summary"  "seed_used"

head(out$combined_field_book)
out$environment_summary         # one row per environment
out$efficiency_summary          # efficiency metrics per environment
out$seed_ledger                 # grams consumed across all final fieldbooks

13.3 Environment-specific design specifications

The env_design_specs list allows each environment to use a different design engine and replication mode. The design field routes to the correct constructor. Additional fields are passed directly as arguments:

env_design_specs <- list(

  # p-rep block design
  Env_A = list(
    design               = "met_prep_famoptg",
    replication_mode     = "p_rep",
    desired_replications = 2L,
    max_prep             = 15L,
    shortage_action      = "downgrade",
    check_treatments     = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
    check_families       = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
    n_blocks             = 4L,
    n_rows               = 10L,
    n_cols               = 12L,
    cluster_source       = "Family"
  ),

  # Row-column alpha design
  Env_B = list(
    design                    = "met_alpha_rc_stream",
    check_treatments          = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
    check_families            = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
    n_reps                    = 2L,
    n_rows                    = 10L,
    n_cols                    = 12L,
    min_block_size            = 10L,
    cluster_source            = "Family"
  ),

  # Augmented repeated-check design
  Env_C = list(
    design           = "met_prep_famoptg",
    replication_mode = "augmented",
    check_treatments = c("CHK1", "CHK2"),
    check_families   = c("CHECK", "CHECK"),
    n_blocks         = 4L,
    n_rows           = 10L,
    n_cols           = 10L,
    cluster_source   = "Family"
  )
)

14. Connectivity and Genomic Prediction: Simulation Illustration

Cross-environment connectivity only matters when genotype performance varies across environments – that is, under genotype-by-environment interaction (G x E). We therefore evaluate designs under a genuine G x E model in which the genotype-by-environment effects have covariance Sigma_E %x% G (a genetic correlation structure across environments, not a single shared breeding value). met_information() returns the coupled across-TPE prediction-error variance (PEV) and reliability (CDmean); simulate_met() returns the realised selection accuracy and genetic gain those designs achieve, together with Monte Carlo standard errors and 95% intervals. When fieldbooks exist, pass their actual treatment-by-environment plot counts through reps; do not substitute an intended average replication.

set.seed(1)
n_geno <- 120
n_env  <- 4
lines  <- paste0("L", seq_len(n_geno))
envs   <- paste0("E", seq_len(n_env))

# Genomic relationship matrix
M  <- matrix(rnorm(n_geno^2), n_geno)
G0 <- tcrossprod(M) / n_geno
diag(G0) <- diag(G0) + 0.5
dimnames(G0) <- list(lines, lines)

# Broad TPE: environments with a mix of positive and negative genetic
# correlations (this is what makes connectivity matter).
Sigma_E <- matrix(c( 1.0,  0.6,  0.2, -0.1,
                     0.6,  1.0,  0.3,  0.0,
                     0.2,  0.3,  1.0,  0.5,
                    -0.1,  0.0,  0.5,  1.0), 4, 4)
dimnames(Sigma_E) <- list(envs, envs)

# Fully balanced positive control: every line in every environment.
alloc_full <- matrix(1L, n_geno, n_env, dimnames = list(lines, envs))

# Random sparse allocation, each line in ~2 of 4 environments.
alloc_sparse <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = lines,
  environments                   = envs,
  allocation_method              = "random_balanced",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 60,
  target_replications            = 2,
  allow_approximate              = TRUE,
  seed                           = 1
)$allocation_matrix

# Equireplicate allocation with correlation-adaptive distinct-treatment
# connectivity. Maximin protects the weakest target-attainment pair.
alloc_eqr <- allocate_sparse_met(
  treatments                     = lines,
  environments                   = envs,
  allocation_method              = "equireplicate",
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 60,
  target_replications            = 2,
  Sigma_E                        = Sigma_E,
  pair_aggregate                 = "maximin",
  seed                           = 1
)$allocation_matrix

# Refine the equireplicate allocation directly against the coupled G x E
# objective (minimise across-TPE PEV).
alloc_opt <- optimize_allocation_gxe(
  alloc_eqr, G = G0, Sigma_E = Sigma_E, iter = 100, seed = 1
)$allocation_matrix

# Design-based coupled PEV / CDmean (lower PEV, higher CDmean is better).
sapply(list(full = alloc_full, sparse = alloc_sparse,
            equireplicate = alloc_eqr, optimised = alloc_opt),
       function(A) met_information(A, G = G0, Sigma_E = Sigma_E)$mean_PEV)

# Realised selection accuracy and genetic gain across the TPE.
sapply(list(full = alloc_full, sparse = alloc_sparse,
            equireplicate = alloc_eqr, optimised = alloc_opt),
       function(A) simulate_met(A, G = G0, Sigma_E = Sigma_E,
                                n_sim = 50, seed = 1)$accuracy_mean)

The fully balanced design is the positive control and information upper bound; its realised Monte Carlo accuracy can still vary. Among the equal-budget sparse options, the comparison tests whether environment-pair balancing and direct optimize_allocation_gxe() refinement improve prediction over plain random sparse allocation. That result must be measured rather than assumed, and its uncertainty should be reported. The next section extends this single-scenario illustration to the covariance, variance, operational, and site-loss perturbations required for a release decision.

15. Benchmarking before field release

The illustration above compares designs under one covariance and one variance setting. A release decision requires a wider validation. The public benchmarking framework provides: (i) known-truth environmental covariance recovery, (ii) leave-year-out and leave-environment-out validation, (iii) full-testing, naive random, M3, and strict-M4 comparators, (iv) paired Monte Carlo evaluation across covariance, variance, and complete site-loss scenarios, (v) missing-environmental-covariate stress tests, and (vi) common-set, capacity, and allocation stability.

reference <- make_met_benchmark_designs(
  treatments = rownames(G0),
  environments = colnames(Sigma_E),
  n_test_entries_per_environment = 60,
  target_replications = 2,
  seed = 2026
)

benchmark <- benchmark_met_designs(
  designs = reference,
  G = G0,
  Sigma_E = Sigma_E,
  sigma_e2 = c(0.5, 1, 2),
  environment_dropout = list(
    none = character(),
    fourth_site_lost = "E4"
  ),
  n_sim = 200,
  seed = 2026
)

benchmark$design_summary
plot_pareto_frontier(benchmark, metric = "accuracy")

The paired simulation exposes every design to the same realised genetic effects and residual standard-normal draws. The Pareto graph uses one vertical endpoint, a 0–100% cost-minimisation axis below, and decreasing real cost above. See vignette("OptiSparseMET-benchmarking") for the complete input contract and demonstrations.

16. Design Component Summary

Component Governing principle Package function(s)
Environmental evidence Keep modalities and interactions separate unless historical responses support calibration build_environment_kernels(), calibrate_environment_covariance()
Environmental grouping Infer and stability-screen group number; retain one network when unsupported infer_mega_environments()
Structural uncertainty Evaluate unweighted alternatives by maximin robustness robust_scenarios()
Capacity verification All treatments must be assignable at least once suggest_safe_k(), min_k_for_full_coverage()
Allocation Balance replication depth against coverage breadth allocate_sparse_met()
Equireplication feasibility ∑eke*=J*r\sum_e k_e^* = J^*r and the degree sequence must be realisable check_equireplicate_feasibility()
Genetic structure Prevent clustering; improve prediction conditions derive_allocation_groups()
Connectivity Count distinct shared genotypes; combine a global common core with correlation-adaptive pairwise overlap while keeping replication separate suggest_common_treatments(), optimize_common_treatments(), allocate_sparse_met()
Seed feasibility One inventory must fund allocation and replication across the network plan_sparse_met_design(), allocate_sparse_met()
Block design Control local heterogeneity within environments met_prep_famoptg()
Row-column design Control spatial gradients in large fixed-grid fields met_alpha_rc_stream()
Efficiency evaluation Quantify design quality before field deployment met_evaluate_famoptg_efficiency(), met_evaluate_alpha_efficiency()
Coupled MET evaluation Use delivered plot counts to quantify PEV, CDmean, accuracy, and gain met_information(), simulate_met()
Empirical benchmarking Compare reference designs with paired truths, operational ledgers, and covariance/variance/site-loss stress tests make_met_benchmark_designs(), benchmark_met_designs()
Environmental validation Quantify covariance recovery, blocked prediction, and missing-covariate sensitivity benchmark_environment_models(), simulate_environment_model_benchmark(), benchmark_environment_missingness()
Decision stability Report common-set, capacity, and allocation reproducibility summarize_design_stability()
Optimisation Search for higher-efficiency arrangements met_optimize_famoptg(), met_optimize_alpha_rc()
Assembly Produce a unified field book for all environments combine_met_fieldbooks(), plan_sparse_met_design()

17. Conclusions

Sparse MET design requires more than balanced incidence. It requires coherent decisions about environmental uncertainty, genetic connectivity, testing breadth, local replication, field geometry, and seed. OptiSparseMET integrates these decisions through four principles: (i) environmental main-effect and interaction kernels remain explicit rather than being collapsed by arbitrary weights; (ii) historical responses calibrate genetic covariance when available, while maximin sensitivity analysis protects decisions when they are not; (iii) common-set size and identity are optimised from binary presence, while local replication is assigned separately from remaining seed; and (iv) delivered plot counts drive information, simulation, and cost.

The resulting workflow supports both random-balanced and equireplicate allocation, additive and optional hybrid-dominance relationships, block-based and row-column local designs, and prediction-oriented evaluation through prediction-error variance (PEV), mean coefficient of determination (CDmean), selection accuracy, and genetic gain. Unsupported environmental grouping falls back to one network, and infeasible allocation or seed demands are reported before deployment.

For plant breeders, the practical output is an auditable trial plan: every genotype-site presence is explicit, every gram of seed is counted once, every local field book respects its geometry, and every design recommendation can be examined against explicit reference designs and plausible quantitative-genetic scenarios before planting.
